description: russia-colonialism techniques used by "Only Pardoned": Alien Rule and the Suppression of Chechen and Ingush National Life (1965-1989), ATT&CK campaign C1182 (v1.0)
name: "Only Pardoned": Alien Rule and the Suppression of Chechen and Ingush National Life (1965-1989) (C1182)

techniques.comment: After the return of the Chechens and the Ingush from exile the USSR did not let the indigenous inhabitants hold key leading posts in government and industry, reserving them for Russian settlers. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "The leading posts (first secretary of the obkom of the CPSU [head of the region's occupation administration], minister of the MVD, republican prosecutor, head of the KGB [predecessor of today's FSB], minister of finance, secretary of the Grozny gorkom of the CPSU [head of the city] and chairman of the Grozny gorispolkom [head of the city administration], head of Grozneft, military commissar of the republic and some others) are reserved for Russian officials"; for the Chechens and the Ingush, 70 % of the population, "roughly 30% of posts were reserved"(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005). According to the letter of 26 communists of 1972, which the historians quote, "in the early 1970s, of the 60 ministries and agencies of the Council of Ministers of the ChIASSR [the Chechen-Ingush republic] only 17 were headed by Chechens or Ingush. In most rural districts the first secretaries of the raikoms [heads of districts] were Russians"(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005). The historians write: "That is precisely why the CC of the CPSU [the central authority in Moscow] keeps sending new first secretaries of the obkom [heads of the region] to Chechen-Ingushetia" - in 1966-1989 these were Apryatkin, Vlasov and Foteev, sent in from other regions(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005). When the Ingush at the rally of January 1973 demanded that locals be appointed to leading posts, Bokov, a leader in the region's occupation administration, replied at a meeting of party functionaries on 21 January: "In their speeches they went so far as to say that a measure should be carried out here to take account of leading cadres from among the Chechens and the Ingush, that is, to carry out indigenisation"(Citation: Общегражданский митинг ингушей 1973 года (публикация архивных документов Чечено-Ингушского обкома КПСС) 2008). Historian A. B. Kuznetsova writes, citing the witness B. Kh. Toriev: "Chechens and Ingush were subjected to harsh discrimination in admission to the CPSU - they were admitted only from among the workers, so that those who held engineering positions were forced to go and work at a factory as labourers in order to be able to join the party"(Citation: Этнополитические процессы в Чечено-Ингушской АССР в 1957-1990 гг. 2005). Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that only by the mid-1980s did Chechens and Ingush head 155 of the 194 village soviets and 11 of the 19 city and district soviets, while "the most significant posts at the middle and republican level, as well as the leadership of Grozny and of the regional committee of the CPSU, remained with the Russian nomenklatura"(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005). The historians write that on 1 July 1989 the region's occupation administration at its meeting "for the first time in the entire history of the Chechen-Ingush party organisation rejected the candidate proposed by the CC of the CPSU (N. I. Semenov) and elected Doku Zavgaev first secretary"(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005).

In 1965-1989 the coloniser, by law and by administrative decisions, kept the Chechens out of the cities and factories of their own republic. The coloniser had restricted the residence registration of Chechens in Grozny as early as 1958; historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "these restrictions in fact ceased to operate only in the 1980s"(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005). Historian A. B. Kuznetsova writes that in the early 1970s "the leadership of the ChIASSR [the Chechen-Ingush republic] (in agreement with the union centre [Moscow]) declared that the labour resources of the republic (read: the unemployed) had to be used locally"(Citation: Этнополитические процессы в Чечено-Ингушской АССР в 1957-1990 гг. 2005). Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "Already in 1979 up to 28% of all able-bodied inhabitants of the Chechen-Ingush ASSR, according to official statistics, derived their main income from work on their personal household plots, that is, were in fact unemployed. Ten years later the level of hidden unemployment, by some estimates, had risen to 40%"(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005).

In 1972-1981 the Chechens and the Ingush twice wrote to Moscow about discrimination and protested on the square; each time the coloniser expelled from the only permitted party and put on trial the protesters, not the region's occupation leadership. Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that in March 1972 26 Chechen and Ingush communists "wrote a collective letter addressed to the CC of the CPSU [the central authority in Moscow], in which they directly accused the party leadership of Chechen-Ingushetia not only of chauvinism but also of corruption. The result of the appeal, however, was not what the authors of the collective letter had counted on: it was not the leaders of the republic who were punished, but they themselves"; S. Bokaev, S. Pliev, N. Umarkhadzhaev, B. Kostoev and B. Lyanov were expelled from the party(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005). On 16 January 1973 the Ingush gathered on the central square of Grozny, in front of the building of the region's occupation administration, and Chechens joined them; rally participant Salman Mamatiev recalls: "on the second day there were almost as many Chechens on the square as Ingush"(Citation: Общегражданский митинг ингушей 1973 года (публикация архивных документов Чечено-Ингушского обкома КПСС) 2008). Eyewitness Aza Bazorkina recalls: "From a makeshift rostrum on Lenin Square, on 16, 17 and 18 January, day and night, the grievance of dispossessed, deceived people pours out", and on the night of 19 January the militia and the internal troops (predecessors of today's Rosgvardiya) cleared the square: "The doubting young people, who did not want to disperse without reliable information, were beaten with rubber truncheons and doused with icy water from fire hoses, herded into buses, driven out of the city and let out there, soaking wet, into a twenty-degree frost in an open field"(Citation: Так это было: национальные репрессии в СССР 1993). On 13 March 1973 Moscow adopted a resolution "On Anti-Social Nationalist Manifestations in the City of Grozny"; on 27 March the region's occupation administration resolved to accept it "for unswerving guidance and execution" and recorded: "For nationalist actions and active participation in anti-social manifestations the following have been expelled from the party: Pliev S. Kh., Gazdiev A. M., as well as Kushtov A. S. - physician at city hospital No. 2, Abadiev B. - director of the puppet theatre, Uzhakhova - teacher at boarding school No. 15, Egiev - former chairman of the construction committee of SMU-7 [trade-union committee of a construction directorate], Daurbekov - former head of department at the Nazran district newspaper"(Citation: Общегражданский митинг ингушей 1973 года (публикация архивных документов Чечено-Ингушского обкома КПСС) 2008). Historian A. B. Kuznetsova gives the tally: "23 people were expelled from the CPSU, 18 from the VLKSM [the Komsomol, the youth organisation of Soviet power], 9 people were removed from leading positions and 14 people were prosecuted"(Citation: Этнополитические процессы в Чечено-Ингушской АССР в 1957-1990 гг. 2005). On 27 December 1973 KGB chairman Andropov (the KGB being the predecessor of today's FSB) reported to Moscow: "After the well-known events that took place in the city of Grozny in January 1973, in which about 400 Ingush from the Prigorodny district of the North Ossetian ASSR took an active part, as a result of measures taken by the state security organs new attempts to carry out socially dangerous acts, especially in February 1973 on the anniversary of the eviction of the Ingush and also on the eve of the holidays of 1 and 9 May, were prevented"(Citation: Записка председателя КГБ СССР Ю. В. Андропова в ЦК КПСС № 3217-А о положении в Чечено-Ингушской АССР после событий января 1973 года 1973). In June 1981 23 communists wrote to Brezhnev about the corruption of Vlasov, head of the region's occupation administration; historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write: "The CC of the CPSU this time too backed the republican leadership, accusing the authors of the letter of nationalism (although among its signatories were people of various nationalities, including Russians and Ukrainians). Two people were expelled from the party"(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005).

From 1973 the coloniser justified the deportation and did not let the Chechens speak of it or of the military seizure of the region, and from 1979 it imposed a "concept" of "the 200th anniversary of the voluntary entry of Chechen-Ingushetia into Russia" and persecuted the historians who disputed it. At a meeting of the region's occupation administration on 27 March 1973 one of its leaders, Bokov, justified the eviction of 1944: "All this, in our view, forced the government to take this extreme measure in order to put an end to the anti-Soviet actions of the political bandit groups [the authorities' name for armed opponents], which found shelter among a significant part of the Chechen-Ingush population", and the minutes of the same meeting named the bearers of "nationalist" ideas one by one: "the writer Khalid Oshaev, expelled from the party, the former deputy director of a plant Kostoev B., the university lecturer and candidate of sciences Vagapov Ya."(Citation: Общегражданский митинг ингушей 1973 года (публикация архивных документов Чечено-Ингушского обкома КПСС) 2008). Historian A. B. Kuznetsova writes that at the discussion of the two-volume "Essays on the History of the Chechen-Ingush ASSR" in 1973 the speakers criticised the "belittling" of the role of the Russian people and the works of the historian V. I. Filkin, "while not a word was said at the discussion about the deportation"(Citation: Этнополитические процессы в Чечено-Ингушской АССР в 1957-1990 гг. 2005). Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that the region's occupation administration launched a persecution of the Chechen intelligentsia "under the guise of a discussion around the 'concept' of the 200th anniversary of the voluntary entry of Chechen-Ingushetia into Russia", whose author was considered to be the archaeologist Vinogradov, and he "relied even on the authority of the CC of the CPSU [the central authority in Moscow]"(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005). In February 1979 L. I. Lavrov, a historian of the Academy of Sciences, wrote on instructions from his superiors a review of the "Justification Memorandum" for the jubilee: the oaths of the 18th century "did not lead to the actual entry of the region into the Russian Empire, since even after the oaths no officials of the tsarist administration appeared there", and "the planned celebration of the jubilee, in the light of the above, appears historically unjustified"; historian V. P. Krikunov, who published the memorandum in 1990, writes: "The first copy of the memorandum got lost and, when the question of whether or not to celebrate the 200th 'jubilee' was being decided, was not taken into account (or rather, it was taken into account, and that, evidently, is why it got lost)"(Citation: Затерянная записка (записка Л. И. Лаврова о «200-летии вхождения Чечено-Ингушетии», февраль 1979) 1990). Historian Viktor Shnirelman writes: "In those years Vinogradov became the chief adviser of the obkom of the CPSU [the region's occupation administration] on ideology and social sciences, which in effect made him the first censor of scholarly and publishing activity in the republic"; "Such Chechen and Ingush historians as M. N. Muzaev, A. Z. Vatsuev, Ya. Z. Akhmadov, Kh. Akiev, Ya. S. Vagapov, Kh. S. Akhmadov and others were subjected to persecution"; the 1977 book by the linguist Kyuri Chokaev, "The Language and History of the Vainakhs", "was declared in the obkom… a model of 'rabid nationalism', and the entire print run was destroyed on the spot"(Citation: Быть аланами: интеллектуалы и политика на Северном Кавказе в XX веке 2006). Historians D. B. Abdurakhmanov and Ya. Z. Akhmadov also write that for disagreeing with the "concept" "there were officially pilloried [publicly disgraced] … the Chechen-Ingush State University lecturer F. P. Bokov, professors N. P. Gritsenko and V. P. Krikunov"(Citation: Битва за Чечню. «Война историографий», или информационная война 2015). Shnirelman writes that Vlasov, head of the region's occupation administration, reproduced the concept "in his speech at the III plenum of the Chechen-Ingush obkom of the CPSU on 14 July 1979" and "gave instructions to propagate it widely in the local media", and in 1982 the jubilee of the "voluntary entry" was combined with the 60th anniversary of the republic: "On this occasion the republic was awarded the Order of the Red Banner of Labour; its leaders received awards too. In particular, Vlasov was presented with the Order of Lenin"(Citation: Быть аланами: интеллектуалы и политика на Северном Кавказе в XX веке 2006). On 29 June 1984 the region's occupation administration recorded in its minutes on the work of the Institute of History, Sociology and Philology: "Vagapov Ya. S., Akhmadov Ya. Z., Vatsuev A. Z. permit themselves politically harmful judgements, dispute the scholarly validity of the concept of the voluntary entry of the Chechens and the Ingush into Russia"(Citation: Битва за Чечню. «Война историографий», или информационная война 2015). Historians D. B. Abdurakhmanov and Ya. Z. Akhmadov write that only in 1990 did "the same organ of the CPSU revoke its decision concerning the institute and its staff as mistaken"(Citation: Битва за Чечню. «Война историографий», или информационная война 2015).

After the return of the Chechens from exile the coloniser did not allow a single mosque to be opened and, through its officials, decided who could pray and where. Muzarov, an official supervising religion, wrote in a report of 25 August 1983: "In Chechen-Ingushetia in the pre-October period [before 1917] Muslim ideology reigned supreme. There were 2,675 mosques, 60 thousand murids [members of religious brotherhoods], 38 sheikhs [religious mentors, heads of brotherhoods], 2,850 mullahs [Islamic clergymen] and 140 religious schools. After the restoration of the republic's autonomy in 1957 it so happened that on the territory of the Chechen-Ingush ASSR there was not a single mosque"(Citation: Отчёт заместителя уполномоченного Совета по делам религий по Чечено-Ингушской АССР Б. А. Музарова о выполнении постановления ЦК КПСС от 5 апреля 1983 г. О мерах по идеологической изоляции реакционной части мусульманского духовенства 1983). The mosques did not vanish by themselves. Most of them the coloniser had closed before the war: historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that religious schools "after the closure of most mosques… moved into the homes of mullahs and Islamic scholars"(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005). Historian Dalkhan Khozhaev writes that during the exile "medieval crypts and pre-revolutionary mosques, tombs and shrines… were blown up"(Citation: Так это было: национальные репрессии в СССР 1993); historians Akhmadov and Khasmagomadov add that in Grozny "the city mosque was destroyed"(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005). The surviving buildings the coloniser took over as clubs and warehouses. On 21 January 1967 277 believers of the Nazran district submitted an application to open a mosque in the village of Barsuki; Asaulka, an official supervising religion, reported to Moscow that the district administration, by its decision of 10 June 1967, had refused "to consider the application on the grounds that, as established by an inspection, 'many signatures under the application were made not by the persons indicated in the application but forged, and the surnames of some persons are fictitious'"(Citation: Информация уполномоченного Совета по делам религий по Чечено-Ингушской АССР А. И. Асаулка о религиозном движении 1967). On 11 November 1969 the government of the region, subordinate to Moscow, in a resolution "On Measures to Strengthen Control over Observance of the Legislation on Religious Cults", recorded that in the districts "ministers of the cult in a number of cases arbitrarily engage in building and opening prayer houses, hold collective rites in public places, organise pilgrimages of believers to so-called 'holy places'", while "effective measures aimed at the gradual cessation of their activity are not being taken"(Citation: Постановление Совета Министров Чечено-Ингушской АССР № 592 О мерах по усилению контроля за соблюдением законодательства о религиозных культах 1969). On 18 May 1977 Bobov, an official supervising religion, reported to Kerimov, the head of that government: "in the republic there are no Muslim religious associations or ministers of the cult registered with the authorities, while at the same time, contrary to the law, 263 Muslim religious societies and groups operate unofficially"(Citation: Справка уполномоченного Совета по делам религий по Чечено-Ингушской АССР Д. П. Бобова председателю Совета Министров ЧИАССР о состоянии религиозного движения 1977). On 19 August 1980 Bobov reported to Moscow: in the republic "there are 62 buildings of former mosques… 17 used as clubs and schools, 25 as storage premises, 8 as factory workshops, post offices, shops, 2 handed over to the use of believers"(Citation: Сведения уполномоченного Совета по делам религий по Чечено-Ингушской АССР Д. П. Бобова о мечетях и их использовании 1980). Historians Ya. Z. Akhmadov and E. Kh. Khasmagomadov write that the region's occupation authorities "directly forbade the opening of mosques in Chechen and Ingush villages, and did not allow the numerous murid [religious] communities to perform religious rites openly either"(Citation: История Чечни в XIX-XX веках 2005).
